a-series-time: Philosopher John McTaggart distinguished two ways of ordering events in time. The A-series orders them by the moving present — past, present, and future — while the B-series orders them by fixed relations of earlier and later. Many hold that our sense of time 'passing' depends on the A-series, while physics describes time the B-series way. The dispute shapes whether the future is as real and fixed as the past.
arendt-totalitarianism: For Hannah Arendt, totalitarianism is a form of rule unlike ordinary dictatorship: it seeks total domination, using terror, ideological myths, and secret police to abolish freedom, spontaneity, and individuality itself. On her view it demands unconditional, unreasoning loyalty and treats people as interchangeable specimens. She saw it as a distinctively modern danger, thriving in mass society and loneliness.
aristotle-potentiality: Aristotle distinguished what a thing is potentially from what it is actually. An acorn is potentially an oak; a child, potentially a rational adult — and these potentials are fixed by each thing's nature, so an acorn cannot become a pumpkin. The pair is a common tool for explaining change and development, and for arguing that unrealized capacities can matter morally.
best-possible-world: Leibniz argued that an all-powerful, all-good God would create the best of infinitely many possible worlds, so evil must somehow fit the best overall arrangement. Voltaire satirized this theodicy — the attempt to justify God's permitting evil — through Dr. Pangloss, who insists all is for the best amid catastrophe. Many now read it as a caution against rationalizing suffering.
capabilities-approach: Developed by Amartya Sen and Martha Nussbaum, the capabilities approach judges lives not by wealth or resources alone but by people's real opportunities to do and be things that matter — being healthy, educated, playing, taking part in community. A resource means little if someone cannot convert it into a functioning life. Many hold it a better yardstick for justice.
cartesian-theater: The Cartesian Theater is Daniel Dennett's name for a tempting but, he argues, mistaken picture of consciousness: that somewhere in the brain everything comes together on an inner stage where a self watches the show. Descartes's split of mind from body encouraged the picture. Dennett's 'multiple drafts' alternative holds there is no single place where experience is finally assembled.
cyborg: A cyborg is a hybrid of organism and machine. Donna Haraway made the cyborg a feminist symbol: a being whose mixed nature dissolves firm boundaries between human and animal, organism and machine, undermining 'natural' categories like gender. Many argue we are already cyborgs — vaccines, pacemakers, and phones are part of us — so the boundary was never clean.
difference-principle: In John Rawls's theory of justice, the difference principle permits social and economic inequalities only when they benefit the least well-off. Rawls derives it from a thought experiment: choose society's rules from behind a 'veil of ignorance,' not knowing which position you will occupy. Inequality is not wrong in itself, on this view, but it must lift those at the bottom.
ecofeminism: Ecofeminism holds that the domination of nature and the domination of women are connected, sharing a common logic that treats both as passive resources for control. Thinkers like Val Plumwood and Carolyn Merchant trace this to a set of dualisms — reason over emotion, culture over nature, man over woman — and argue that environmental crises cannot be solved without dismantling them.
eugenics: Eugenics is the project of improving a human population by controlling who reproduces, encouraging 'desirable' traits and discouraging 'undesirable' ones. Twentieth-century programs included forced sterilization, and the 'eu' (good) in eugenics quietly smuggles in a judgment about which lives count as good stock. The central moral question is who decides which traits count, and by what right.
family-resemblance: Wittgenstein observed that some concepts resist definition by fixed conditions shared by all their instances. 'Game' is his example: board games, ball games, and solitaire share no single common feature, only overlapping, criss-crossing similarities, like faces in one family. He argued many words work this way — learned through examples rather than strict definitions.
frankl-meaning: Viktor Frankl, a psychiatrist who survived the Nazi camps, argued that our deepest drive is meaning, not pleasure or power. His logotherapy holds that life can have meaning even amid unavoidable suffering, since we keep the freedom to choose our stance toward our conditions. Even mundane tasks, on this view, become bearable when tied to a purpose beyond the self.
heteronormativity: Heteronormativity is the background assumption that heterosexuality and fixed male–female roles are the natural default, so taken for granted that it structures institutions unnoticed. Many argue, with Judith Butler's influence, that this norm is culturally produced rather than natural, marginalizing gay, lesbian, bisexual, and transgender people and policing everyone's behavior. The term names the expectation itself, not merely individual prejudice.
kant-perpetual-peace: In Perpetual Peace (1795), Kant set out conditions for lasting peace among states: republican constitutions, a federation of free states, and universal hospitality — a stranger's right not to be treated as an enemy on foreign ground. He condemned colonial conquest and argued peace is a duty reason imposes, not a mere hope. The League of Nations and the UN echo his plan.
last-man: In Thus Spoke Zarathustra, Nietzsche's 'last man' is the opposite of the overhuman: a comfortable, risk-averse creature who wants only security and small pleasures, having abandoned all striving after the death of old values. Nietzsche presented this as modernity's danger — contentment without greatness. The figure is often used to critique cultures that trade aspiration for comfort.
liar-paradox: The Liar Paradox arises from a sentence like 'This sentence is false': if it is true it is false, and if false then true. It drove major twentieth-century work on truth, suggesting an ordinary notion of truth is inconsistent, and proposed fixes tend to relocate rather than remove the problem.
purity-and-danger: In Purity and Danger, anthropologist Mary Douglas argued that dirt is 'matter out of place' — not an absolute property but a violation of an order we impose. What counts as filthy tracks what a culture counts as orderly, so purity rules express social boundaries. Anxieties about contamination, on this view, often mark a group treated as out of place.
soul-making-theodicy: Soul-making theodicy, developed by John Hick, answers why an all-good God permits suffering: hardship and real choice make the world a 'valley of soul-making,' where free beings grow into virtues like courage and compassion. God keeps an 'epistemic distance' so goodness is never coerced. Critics reply that some suffering seems far beyond what character formation could require.
stoic-indifferents: The Stoics held that only virtue is truly good; health, wealth, and reputation are 'indifferents' — nothing to happiness. Still, they distinguished 'preferred indifferents,' like health, which accord with nature and are rational to pursue — so long as one is not enslaved to them. Losing wealth or status cannot harm a good person, though preferring otherwise is reasonable.
stream-of-consciousness: William James described mental life as a 'stream of consciousness': an ever-flowing current of thoughts and feelings rather than a chain of separate ideas, with each mind selecting from the 'blooming, buzzing confusion' of experience. The phrase also names a literary technique that narrates a character's unfiltered inner flow, trying to put readers inside that current.
twin-earth: In Hilary Putnam's Twin Earth thought experiment, a distant planet is just like Earth except that its 'water' is a different liquid, indistinguishable in appearance. A person there and her Earthly twin mean different things by 'water,' though their inner mental states are exactly alike. Meanings, Putnam concluded, are not in the head — words depend partly on the world for what they mean.
underdetermination: Underdetermination of theory by evidence is the claim that data alone never pin down a single theory: several incompatible explanations can fit the same observations equally well. Choice among them must then rest on values like simplicity or explanatory power, which the evidence itself does not dictate. Many hold this makes scientific inference less mechanical than it looks.
vindication-women: In A Vindication of the Rights of Woman (1792), Mary Wollstonecraft argued that women seem inferior only because they are denied education and trained to please men. She demanded equal education and recognition of women as rational persons, against Rousseau's ideal of the docile helpmate. The book became a founding feminist text, insisting that virtue and reason have no sex.
wheel-of-fortune: The Wheel of Fortune is a medieval image, made famous by Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, of fortune as a spinning wheel: prosperity and ruin, rise and fall, succeed one another with no stability for those clinging to the rim. Boethius's remedy is to move to the wheel's motionless center — the eternal and unchanging — since what Fortune gives she can take away.
